subject: mathematics
question_text: Show that the determinant with rows (b+c, c+a, a+b), (a+b, b+c, c+a) and (a, b, c) is a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc.

mark_split.label: Add R₃ to R₁ and take (a+b+c) out

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.42, chapter 5 MATRICES, Short Answer question 11. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1+1+1 shape gives one mark each to the two row operations, the expansion, and the standard identity that finishes it. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B runs Q11 to Q18 at 4 marks each, answer any 6 of 8, under the 2026-27 pattern; Matrices carries a Section B slot and also appears in Section C. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this one — name each row operation and the identity at the end.

steps.label: Add R₃ to R₁ and take (a+b+c) out
steps.margin_note: First mark. Add R₃ to R₁ and every entry of R₁ turns into the same expression a + b + c, which can then be taken outside. The answer already contains that factor.
steps.memory_tip: R₁ + R₃ makes every entry of the top row a + b + c, and that factor comes straight out.
lines: Let Δ be the given determinant:

lines.text: \Delta = \begin{vmatrix} b+c & c+a & a+b \\ a+b & b+c & c+a \\ a & b & c \end{vmatrix}

lines: Apply R₁ → R₁ + R₃. Every entry of R₁
becomes a + b + c, so it comes out:

lines.text: \Delta = (a+b+c)\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ a+b & b+c & c+a \\ a & b & c \end{vmatrix}

recall.must_convey: That R₁ → R₁ + R₃ makes the top row constant at a+b+c, which is taken outside.
accept: add the third row to the first row
every entry of the first row becomes a plus b plus c so take it out

the top row turns into all ones after the factor comes out

steps.why: Adding one row to another leaves the value unchanged, and a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc has (a+b+c) as a factor — so producing that factor early is the natural first move.
common_mistakes: Expanding the 3×3 determinant directly, which gives a long expression that is hard to factorise.
Taking (a+b+c) out of a row where the entries are not all equal to it.

steps.label: Simplify R₂ by R₂ − R₃
steps.margin_note: Second mark. R₂ − R₃ removes a from the first entry, b from the second and c from the third, leaving the short row (b, c, a).
steps.memory_tip: R₂ − R₃ turns (a+b, b+c, c+a) into the short row (b, c, a).

lines.text: \Delta = (a+b+c)\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ b & c & a \\ a & b & c \end{vmatrix}

recall.must_convey: That R₂ → R₂ − R₃ reduces the middle row to (b, c, a).
accept: subtract the third row from the second row
the middle row becomes b, c, a
apply R two minus R three to shorten the second row
R two minus R three cheste b c a vasthundi
a plus b minus a is b, so the row becomes single letters

steps.why: Each entry of R₂ is a sum of two letters, and the entry below it is one of those two. Subtracting leaves a single letter, which makes the expansion short.
common_mistakes: Subtracting in the wrong direction and getting (−b, −c, −a).
Forgetting that the factor (a+b+c) stays outside during this operation.

steps.label: Expand the determinant
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The top row is all 1s, so expanding along it is the easiest route. Keep the + − + signs: the middle term is subtracted.
steps.memory_tip: A top row of all 1s makes the expansion three small 2×2 determinants.

recall.must_convey: That expanding along the row of 1s gives (a+b+c)(a²+b²+c²−ab−bc−ca).
accept: expand along the first row of ones
the three minors give a squared plus b squared plus c squared minus ab minus bc minus ca
keep the plus minus plus signs so the middle term is subtracted
ones unna row along expand cheyyali
it becomes a plus b plus c into the second bracket
heard_as: a squared plus b squared plus c squared
minus ab minus bc minus ca

steps.why: With 1s along the top row each cofactor is just a 2×2 determinant, and the three of them collect into the second bracket of the standard identity.
common_mistakes: Using + + + and so getting +bc instead of −bc.
Collecting only two of the three cross terms ab, bc and ca.

steps.label: Apply the standard identity
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The two brackets are exactly the standard factorisation of a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc, so the proof ends by naming it — no further multiplying out is needed.
steps.memory_tip: (a+b+c)(a²+b²+c²−ab−bc−ca) is the standard form of a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc.

recall.must_convey: That (a+b+c)(a²+b²+c²−ab−bc−ca) is the standard factorisation of a³+b³+c³−3abc, finishing the proof.

steps.why: The identity is standard algebra from an earlier class. Recognising it saves multiplying two brackets out and reaching the same nine terms the long way.
common_mistakes: Multiplying the brackets out and stopping before the six cross terms cancel.
Writing the second bracket as a² + b² + c² + ab + bc + ca.
